intro: Four short modules take you from your first commands to writing and running your own scripts. Each has a study guide, tips, key terms and slides. Practice every skill in the Labs tab, where a simulated terminal checks your work.

modules.title: Shells and navigation
modules.summary: Know what a shell is, how Bash, PowerShell and the Windows command prompt differ, and how to move around, get help and work faster with history and completion.

guide.html: A shell is a program that reads the commands you type, runs them, and prints the result. The window you type in is the terminal; the shell is the program inside it. Typing is faster than clicking once you know a few commands, it can be repeated exactly, and it is the only way to manage most servers.

• Bash (and the similar sh, zsh) is the default on Linux and the Terminal on macOS. Commands print text.
  • PowerShell is built into Windows and also runs on Linux and macOS. Its commands, called cmdlets, are named Verb-Noun (Get-ChildItem) and pass objects, not just text.
  • Command Prompt (cmd.exe) is the older Windows shell with commands like dir, ipconfig and copy.

The ideas are the same in all three: a command, options, and arguments.

Most commands look like command -options arguments. In ls -l /etc, ls is the command, -l is an option that changes how it behaves, and /etc is the argument it works on. PowerShell uses named parameters instead: Get-ChildItem -Path C:\Users -Force.

Spaces separate the parts, so a name with a space needs quotes: cd "My Documents".

Every shell has a current directory (working folder). pwd prints it, ls lists it, and cd changes it.

  • Absolute path starts at the top: /var/log (Linux) or C:\Windows (Windows).
  • Relative path starts from where you are: ../logs. . means here and .. means one level up.
  • ~ means your home folder in Bash. cd with no argument also goes home.

PowerShell equivalents: Get-Location (pwd), Get-ChildItem (ls, dir), Set-Location (cd).

Nobody memorizes every option. Use the built-in help: man ls (full manual, q to quit), ls --help (short summary), or Get-Help Get-ChildItem -Examples in PowerShell.

Speed tricks that work in every shell: Tab completes names, the Up arrow brings back earlier commands, history lists them, Ctrl+C stops a running command and Ctrl+L clears the screen. Be careful, though: the shell does what you type, with no undo.

tips: Tab completion saves typing and prevents typos in long paths.
Linux is case-sensitive: Notes.txt and notes.txt are different files. Windows is not.
If a command seems to hang, Ctrl+C usually stops it.
Read before you press Enter, especially on commands that delete or overwrite.
Look up unknown options with man or --help before guessing.
terms: The window where you type; the shell runs inside it.
The program that interprets commands (Bash, PowerShell, cmd).
The folder commands act on by default.
A full path from the root, such as /var/log.
A path measured from the current directory.
Changes how a command behaves, such as -l.
What the command acts on, such as a file name.

modules.title: Files and folders
modules.summary: Create, copy, move, rename and delete files and folders safely, use wildcards, find hidden files, and read permissions.

guide.html:
TaskBashPowerShell

Create an empty filetouch notes.txtNew-Item notes.txt
Copycp a.txt b.txtCopy-Item a.txt b.txt
Move or renamemv old.txt new.txtMove-Item old.txt new.txt

Show contentscat notes.txtGet-Content notes.txt

guide.h: Copy, move and the options that matter
guide.html:
cp leaves the original; mv does not, and it is also how you rename. Copying a folder needs -r (recursive): cp -r projects backup. mkdir -p a/b/c creates every missing folder in the path in one go.

ls -l shows details (permissions, owner, size, date) and ls -a includes hidden files, which begin with a dot such as .bashrc. Combine them: ls -la.

The shell expands wildcards before the command runs. * matches any characters, ? matches exactly one, and [ab] matches one of the listed characters. ls *.txt lists every text file; cp report-?.csv backup/ copies report-1.csv but not report-10.csv.

Tip: run ls with the same pattern first to see exactly what a wildcard will match before you use it with rm.

There is no recycle bin on the command line. rm deletes immediately and rm -r deletes a folder and everything inside. Habits that prevent disasters:

  • Run ls with the same path or pattern first.
  • Use rm -i to be asked about each file.
  • Never run a recursive delete as root unless you have double-checked the path.
  • Keep backups of anything you cannot recreate.

In ls -l output, -rwxr-xr-- has a type character then three groups: owner (rwx), group (r-x) and everyone else (r--). r = read, w = write, x = execute (run, or enter a folder).

chmod changes them. Numbers add up: read 4, write 2, execute 1. So chmod 755 script.sh is rwxr-xr-x, and chmod 600 secret.txt is rw-------. chmod +x script.sh makes a script runnable.

tips: Add -r to copy or delete folders.
mv is rename and move in one command.
Hidden files start with a dot; use ls -a to see them.
Check a wildcard with ls before using it with rm.
Scripts need the execute bit (chmod +x) before you can run them.
terms: Applies to a folder and everything inside it (-r).
A pattern such as * or ? expanded by the shell.
A name starting with a dot, hidden from plain ls.
Read, write and execute rights for owner, group and others.

modules.title: Pipes, filters and logs
modules.summary: Chain small commands with pipes, redirect output to files, and use grep, sort, uniq, cut, head and wc to answer questions from log files.

guide.html:
Every command has a standard input, a standard output (normal results) and a standard error (error messages). Redirection sends them to or from files:

  • > writes output to a file, replacing it: ls > files.txt
  • >> appends to the end of the file
  • 2> redirects error messages: cmd 2> errors.txt

Careful: a single > silently overwrites an existing file.

The pipe | sends one command's output into the next command's input. Small tools that each do one job combine into a powerful one-liner:

cat access.log | grep 404 | wc -l

reads the log, keeps lines containing 404, and counts them.

ToolWhat it does
grep text fileKeep lines that match (-i ignore case, -v invert, -c count)
cut -d" " -f1Take one field from each line
sortSort lines (-n numeric, -r reverse)
uniq -cCollapse repeated adjacent lines and count them (sort first!)
head -n 5 / tail -n 5First or last lines (tail -f follows a growing log)
wc -lCount lines

Which client IP address made the most requests? The IP is the first field in each line:

cut -d" " -f1 access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3

Cut out the IP, sort so duplicates sit together, count each one, sort the counts from high to low, and keep the top three. Build pipelines one step at a time, checking the output at each pipe.

PowerShell pipes objects, so you filter by property instead of cutting text:

Get-Process | Where-Object CPU -gt 100 | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 5 Name, CPU

Useful partners: Where-Object (filter), Sort-Object, Select-Object (choose properties or the first N), Group-Object (count by value), Measure-Object (count/sum), and Export-Csv or Out-File to save results. Log search: Select-String -Path app.log -Pattern ERROR.

tips: Sort before uniq: uniq only collapses neighbouring duplicates.
> overwrites, >> appends.
grep -c counts matching lines; wc -l counts all lines.
Build a pipeline one stage at a time and check the output as you go.
Quote search text containing spaces: grep "failed login" auth.log.

modules.title: Writing and running scripts
modules.summary: Turn commands into reusable scripts: shebang and permissions, variables, conditions, loops, arguments, exit codes, and the habits that keep scripts safe.

guide.html: A script is a text file of commands that run in order. Script anything you do more than twice: backups, cleaning old files, collecting information for tickets, creating accounts. Scripts are faster, repeatable and less error-prone than doing it by hand, and they document how a task is done.

#!/bin/bash
# backup.sh: copy the projects folder to a dated archive
SRC="$HOME/projects"
DEST="$HOME/backup-$(date +%F).tar.gz"
tar -czf "$DEST" "$SRC"
echo "Backup written to $DEST"
  • The first line, the shebang #!/bin/bash, says which interpreter runs the file.
  • # starts a comment.
  • NAME=value sets a variable (no spaces around =); $NAME reads it. Use double quotes so spaces do not break it.
  • $(command) captures a command's output.

Make it runnable and run it: chmod +x backup.sh then ./backup.sh.

#!/bin/bash
if [ ! -d "$1" ]; then
  echo "Usage: $0 FOLDER" >&2
  exit 1
fi
for f in "$1"/*.log; do
  echo "Checking $f"
  grep -c ERROR "$f"
done
  • $1, $2 are the arguments; $0 is the script name; $# is the count.
  • if [ test ]; then ... fi makes decisions. Common tests: -f file exists, -d folder exists, -z string empty, -eq numbers equal.
  • for x in list; do ... done repeats for each item.
  • Exit codes: every command returns a number, 0 = success, anything else = failure. $? holds the last one, and exit 1 ends your script with failure.

param([string]$Path = "C:\Logs")
$old = Get-ChildItem $Path -File |
  Where-Object LastWriteTime -lt (Get-Date).AddDays(-30)
if ($old) { $old | Remove-Item -WhatIf }
else { Write-Host "Nothing to clean" }

Variables start with $, param() declares inputs, and -WhatIf shows what would happen without doing it. Scripts are .ps1 files. Windows blocks them by default through the execution policy; Get-ExecutionPolicy shows it, and RemoteSigned is a common, reasonable setting. It is a safety guard, not a security boundary.

• Test first on a copy or in a lab. Use echo in front of a risky command (or -WhatIf) to see what it would do.
  • Never hard-code passwords or keys in a script; read them from a protected file or a secrets manager.
  • Quote variables so a space or empty value cannot turn rm -r $DIR/ into rm -r /.
  • Check results: test exit codes, print clear errors, and fail early. In Bash, set -eu stops on errors and unset variables.
  • Least privilege: do not run scripts as root or Administrator unless needed.
  • Comment the why, keep scripts in version control, and schedule with cron (Linux) or Task Scheduler (Windows).

tips: No spaces around = when assigning Bash variables.
Quote variables: "$VAR".
A script needs the execute bit before ./script.sh works.
0 means success; non-zero means failure.
Test with echo or -WhatIf before running anything destructive.
Do not put passwords in scripts.
terms: First line naming the interpreter, e.g. #!/bin/bash.
A named value: NAME=value, read with $NAME.
Number returned by a command; 0 means success.
A value passed to the script when you run it.
